extracted.intended_audience: students and citizens studying Virginia government and constitutional history
extracted.subtask_short: Virginia Bill of Rights and government structure
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and explain Virginia constitutional provisions: the Bill of Rights, voter qualifications and procedures, and the organization and powers/limits of the legislative, executive and judicial departments, including county formation rules. This is a civics/textbook treatment aimed at learners of state government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers and term-limited office-holding
rubrics_metrics.description: "That the legislative, executive and judicial departments of the State should be separate and distinct; and that the members thereof may be restrained from oppression, by feeling and participating the burthens of the people, they should, at fixed periods, be reduced to a private station, return into that body from which they were originally taken, and the vacancies be supplied by regular elections, in which all or any part of the former members shall be again eligible, or ineligible, as the laws may direct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: organize the three departments as separate, independent departments; officials have specific terms and return to private status at end of terms; re‑eligibility is governed by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free elections and suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: "That all elections ought to be free; and that all men having sufficient evidence of permanent common interest with, and attachment to, the community, have the right of suffrage..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All elections should be free and open; regular residents with permanent interest in the community have the right to vote; taxation or taking of property for public uses requires consent of the people or their representatives; people cannot be bound by laws they have not assented to via themselves or elected representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on suspending laws without representatives' consent
rubrics_metrics.description: "That all power of suspending laws, or the execution of laws, by any authority, without consent of the representatives of the people, is injurious to their rights and ought not to be exercised."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No office-holder should have authority to suspend laws or their execution independent of the representatives of the citizenry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights in criminal prosecutions (due process and jury rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That in criminal prosecutions a man hath a right to demand the cause and nature of his accusation, to be confronted with the accusers and witnesses, to call for evidence in his favor, and to a speedy trial by an impartial jury of his vicinage, without whose unanimous consent he cannot be found guilty... nor be compelled in any criminal proceeding to give evidence against himself, nor be put twice in jeopardy for the same offense...."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guarantees: notice of charges, confrontation of accusers/witnesses, ability to present evidence, speedy impartial jury trial by local jury (unanimous verdict required), protection from deprivation of life/liberty except by law or judgment of peers, protection against self-incrimination and double jeopardy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of excessive bail, fines, and cruel punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: "That excessive bail ought not to be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bail, fines and punishments must be reasonable and not cruel or unusual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warrant specificity; ban on general warrants
rubrics_metrics.description: "That general warrants, whereby an officer or messenger may be commanded to search suspected places without evidence of a fact committed, or to seize any person or persons not named... are grievous and oppressive, and ought not to be granted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search warrants must state specifically the exact place to be searched or the individual to be seized, and the offense should be specified and supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process and jury trial preference in property controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: "That no person shall be deprived of his property without due process of law; and in controversies respecting property, and in suits between man and man, trial by jury is preferable to any other, and ought to be held sacred."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property cannot be taken without due legal process; jury trial is preferred in property disputes. The General Assembly may set minimum juror numbers in civil cases (not less than five in cases cognizable by justices of the peace, or not less than seven otherwise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the press and speech (responsibility for abuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That the freedom of the press is one of the great bulwarks of liberty... and any citizen may freely speak, write and publish his sentiments on all subjects, being responsible for the abuse of that right."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates freedom of speech and press while noting individuals are responsible for abuses (e.g., libel, incitement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia as defense and civilian control of military
rubrics_metrics.description: "That a well-regulated militia, composed of the body of the people, trained to arms, is the proper, natural and safe defense of a free State; that standing armies, in time of peace, should be avoided as dangerous to liberty; and that in all cases the military should be under strict subordination to, and governed by, the civil power."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militia of the people preferred for defense; standing peacetime armies are dangerous; military must be subordinate to civil authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to uniform state government (no internal separate governments)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That the people have a right to uniform government; and, therefore, that no government separate from, or independent of, the government of Virginia, ought to be erected or established within the limits thereof."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No separate or independent government within the state should be erected; state governance should be uniform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues required to preserve free government
rubrics_metrics.description: "That no free government, or the blessings of liberty can be preserved to any people, but by a firm adherence to justice, moderation, temperance, frugality and virtue, and by frequent recurrence to fundamental principles."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral principles (justice, moderation, temperance, frugality, virtue) and a return to fundamentals are necessary to preserve liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of religion and non-coercion in worship
rubrics_metrics.description: "That religion or the duty which we owe to our Creator, and the manner of discharging it, can be directed only by reason and conviction, not by force or violence; and, therefore, all men are equally entitled to the free exercise of religion, according to the dictates of conscience..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious exercise must be free, directed by reason/conscience not coercion; mutual duty to forbearance and charity is urged; government must not coerce religious practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration of rights not exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: "The rights enumerated in this bill of rights shall not be construed to limit other rights of the people not therein expressed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed rights do not deny or deny the existence of other rights held by the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter qualification: United States citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: A voter must be a citizen of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the enumerated prerequisites for suffrage in the state constitution/text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter qualification: age requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A voter must be at least twenty-one years of age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimum age qualification for voting at the time described in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter qualification: one-year Virginia residency
rubrics_metrics.description: A voter must be a resident of Virginia at least one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State residency requirement prior to voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter qualification: six-month local residency
rubrics_metrics.description: A voter must be a resident of the county, city or town at least six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local residency requirement in the jurisdiction where the voter votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter qualification: precinct residency (30 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: A voter must be a resident of the voting precinct at least thirty days prior to the election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term precinct residency requirement immediately preceding an election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter registration prerequisite: payment of poll tax
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment of an annual state capitation or poll tax of one dollar and fifty cents to the county or city treasurer at least six months prior to the election; the receipt of such payment is necessary for registration before voting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poll tax payment was required for registration; non‑voting eligible residents who refrained from voting must pay for up to three prior years; new residents pay pro rata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter qualification: literacy test
rubrics_metrics.description: The passing of a literacy test to prove one's ability to read and write in English and to understand the functions of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A literacy requirement was part of voter qualification as described in the historical text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter registration procedure and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper registration at least 30 days before the election at the office of the local Registrar of Elections which includes presentation of one's poll tax receipt, the filling in of certain required forms pertaining to personal history and the swearing under oath of the truth of one's statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration was (at the time) permanent once properly completed; active U.S. Armed Forces members are exempt from poll tax and registration prerequisites and may have poll taxes cancelled for three prior years after honorable discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualifications from voting/registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain persons are excluded from registering and voting: idiots, insane persons, paupers, persons disqualified by crime or specific disabilities which have not been removed, persons convicted of treason, felony, bribery, petit larceny, obtaining money or property under false pretenses, embezzlement, forgery or perjury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The General Assembly may remove such disabilities by a two-thirds vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret ballot and polling place procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: All elections by the people are by secret ballot. Election officials are sworn in; one judge opens the ballot box publicly to show emptiness, locks it until polls close; voters are checked for registration and poll tax receipt; voters mark ballots alone in booths and fold them, then hand them to a judge who places them in the box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintains secrecy and integrity: illegal to approach a voter nearer than 100 feet of polling place; 15-minute and closing-time announcement procedure; improper/defaced ballots may be challenged and thrown out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot handling, counting, tallying and recount procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: After polls close, unused ballots placed in special envelope; used ballots tipped out and checked; representatives of political parties may observe; election clerks make two sets of tally sheets and keep personal tallies; the 'tally' method with diagonal fifth line used; disagreements trigger a complete recount for that candidate; tie votes decided by the Election Board (often by coin flip).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An official written report is prepared on the back of each poll book, signed by election judges and clerks; poll books and ballots submitted to county/city clerk and reviewed by Board of Elections; successful candidates receive certificate of election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for office-holding
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person qualified to vote is eligible to any office of the State, county, city or other subdivision of the State wherein he resides except as stated otherwise in the State Constitution. Persons eighteen years of age are eligible to the office of notary public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms of officers begin on Feb 1 following their election unless otherwise stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers principle (constitutional prohibition on exercising others' powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither department shall 'exercise the powers properly belonging to either of the others nor may any person exercise the power of more than one of them at the same time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforces institutional separation: no person may concurrently exercise powers of different branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Assembly composition: Senate size and term
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution requires that the Senate consist of not more than forty and not less than thirty-three members, elected quadrennially... term of office is four years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senators are elected by voters of Senatorial Districts on the first Tuesday following the first Monday in November of every other odd-numbered year in which the Governor is not elected.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Assembly composition: House of Delegates size and term
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Delegates consist of not more than one hundred and not less than ninety members... term of office is two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegates are elected on the Tuesday following the first Monday in November of every odd-numbered year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Districting and reapportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Districts (Senatorial and House) are set up by the General Assembly; reapportionment or redistricting must take place every ten years to offset population changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A special commission appointed by the governor does districting; district numbers and entitlements to members described; congressional districts must be contiguous and compact and as nearly equal in inhabitants as practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dual office-holding for General Assembly members
rubrics_metrics.description: No General Assembly member can hold any other public office at the same time or be elected by this assembly to any civil office of profit in the state during his term. Likewise, holders of certain federal or state salaried offices or specified positions cannot be members during continuance in office; if elected, former office must be vacated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two constitutional requirements: be a qualified voter and live in the district represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative salaries and anti-self-enrichment timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Salaries of members are fixed by law and paid from the public treasury. Any act providing an increase of legislative salary cannot take effect until the end of the term for which the members voting thereon were elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a check against legislators voting immediate pay increases for themselves; examples of amounts at time of writing are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular session timing, length and extension rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly meets at Richmond in regular session once every two years on the second Wednesday in January in even-numbered years. The maximum number of days in the regular session is sixty, but a session may be extended not longer than thirty days if three-fifths of the members of each house concur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special sessions may be called by the Governor or at request of two-thirds of members of both houses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quorum, adjournment and attendance powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A quorum is necessary to do business and a majority of the members of each house is considered a quorum. However, a small number may adjourn from day to day and they have the power to compel the attendance of members according to the rules established by each house individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each house sets rules to compel attendance; neither house can, without the consent of the other, adjourn to another place nor for more than three days while a session is in progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: House organization, officers and journal-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: The House must organize at outset; Clerk of previous House serves until new chairman chosen; each house selects its own officers (Clerk, Sergeant-at-Arms, Door Keepers), settles rules of procedure and keeps a journal of proceedings which must be published from time to time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-fifth of members present may demand 'yeas' and 'nays' be entered in journal; Clerk is responsible for payroll, docket, and printing of legislative acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill-to-law process (six major steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Six major steps: (1) Origination in either house; sponsor called 'Patron' and appropriations customarily in House; (2) Bill referred to proper committee for consideration; (3) Bill printed and first reading (title only); (4) Second reading: full reading, patron explains, discussion, amendments, engrossing with amendments; (5) Third reading: final passage in both houses by recorded roll call with required participation; (6) Enrollment: printed in final form and signed by presiding officers then sent to Governor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No regular bill can be introduced after the last three weeks of a session; conference committees resolve differences; passage requires majority of ayes of those voting but at least two-fifths of members elected must participate in voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency and appropriation law exceptions to effective-date rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of an emergency measure, a recorded 'aye' vote of four-fifths of the members voting in each house may result in omission of the usual required printing and reading. General appropriation laws and emergency laws may be made effective earlier than the usual period by four-fifths recorded vote to state the time they take effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally a law cannot take effect until at least ninety days after adjournment of the session in which it was enacted, with the stated exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-subject and title requirements for laws; revival/amendment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Each law can include only one subject or object, and such subject or object must be expressed in its title. In order to revive or amend a law, the title reference alone cannot be used; the act revived or the section amended must be re-enacted and published at length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents use of misleading titles to effect unrelated changes or to resurrect prior acts without full re-enactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority requirement for bills creating offices or affecting public monies
rubrics_metrics.description: A recorded affirmative vote by a majority of all the members elected to each house is necessary for passing any bills which create or establish a new office, which create, continue or revive a debt or charge, or which concern public monies or taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher threshold applies to fiscal and office-creation legislation; all tax bills must state tax requirements clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment procedure and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Delegates has the right to bring impeachment charges; such charges are prosecuted before the Senate which has the sole power to try impeachments. A two-thirds affirmative vote of the senators present is necessary for conviction. Penalties include removal from office and disqualification from further office-holding; criminal indictment and trial may also follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate may try impeachments during recess if charges are preferred before adjournment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment, election and confirmation powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly elects judges of the Supreme Court of the State when terms expire and judges of circuit, corporate and chancery courts. The Governor appoints executive department heads, but appointments generally must be approved by the General Assembly; commission member appointments must be confirmed or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative confirmation plays a role in state appointments and judicial selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional apportionment and districting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures have the power to divide their states into Congressional election districts. These districts must 'be composed of contiguous (adjacent) and compact territory containing as nearly as practicable, an equal number of inhabitants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides fair district design by contiguity, compactness, and equal population considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: suspension of habeas corpus (limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot suspend the writ of habeas corpus unless when, in case of invasion or rebellion, such action is required for public safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habeas corpus protects against unlawful detention and guarantees right to immediate court hearing to assess detention grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: bill of attainder
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot pass a bill of attainder (an act pronouncing sentence without trial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guarantees that individuals are not punished without a trial by jury with proper jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: ex post facto laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot pass an ex post facto law (one which makes previously innocent action criminal and punishes it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retroactive criminal laws detrimental to accused persons are barred; retroactive laws favorable to accused (reducing penalty) are permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: laws impairing the obligation of contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot pass a law impairing the obligation of contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts are protected from legislative acts that would weaken enforceability or impair obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: abridging freedom of speech or of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot pass a law abridging the freedom of speech or of the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom to engage in political discussion and criticism is protected though not absolute (limitations on untruths, incitement, defamation, aiding enemies in war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: taking private property without just compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot enact a law whereby private property would be taken or damaged for public uses without just compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The General Assembly defines 'public uses'; in disputes over fair value, the court decides the amount. This is the state's eminent domain protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: compelling religious practice or tests
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot compel an individual to frequent or support a particular religious place of worship and cannot force an individual to suffer because of his religious beliefs or opinions; it cannot require religious tests or confer privileges to a particular sect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious freedom protections echo Jefferson's statute; forbids authorizing an official church or taxing for church support; forbids incorporation/charters for denominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: lotteries and gambling
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly is forbidden to authorize lotteries or to allow residents to buy, sell, or transfer lottery tickets or chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State prohibits legislative authorization of lotteries as a matter of public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: County formation, division and consolidation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A new county must have a minimum area of 600 square miles and the county or counties from which it is formed cannot be less than 600 square miles after the new county has been formed. No county can be reduced in population below 8,000 people. Whenever any county has a length three times its breadth, or has a length exceeding fifty miles, it may be divided at the discretion of the General Assembly. The General Assembly may consolidate existing counties upon approval of a majority of the qualified voters of each county in a specific election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets quantitative thresholds for county creation and population/area constraints; consolidation requires local voter approval.
